An ACI container runs a nightly data-processing job that should exit when it's done. If the process fails with a non-zero exit code, ACI should restart it. If it succeeds, it must not run again.

Which restart policy should you set?
items.answerText: D — OnFailure
items.expl:
Correct answer: D — OnFailure

OnFailure restarts containers only when they exit with an error, which suits run-to-completion tasks that should retry on failure.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — Manual: isn't an ACI restart policy value.
  • B — Never: won't retry after a failure.
  • C — Always: the default; it restarts containers even after successful completion, rerunning the job.

You plan to manage licenses for 1,200 users by using groups. The licensing team suggests assigning a license to a group named All-Staff whose members are the groups HR, Sales, and Ops (nested groups).

items.answerText: D — They will not receive the license because group-based licensing applies only to direct members

Correct answer: D — They will not receive the license because group-based licensing applies only to direct members

Group-based licensing evaluates the direct members of the licensed group. Nested group membership isn't expanded for licensing, so users in HR, Sales, and Ops receive nothing from All-Staff. Assign the license to each group directly, or make All-Staff a dynamic group that contains the users.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — They will receive the license only if All-Staff is a Microsoft 365 group: the group type doesn't change the direct-member rule.
  • B — They will receive the license because licensing is inherited through nesting: this is the common misconception the question tests; nesting is not supported for licensing.
  • C — They will receive the license only after a manual reprocess: reprocessing re-evaluates direct members; it doesn't make nested membership count.

items.stem:
Subnet snet-web has this effective route table:

Source   Address prefix   Next hop type        Next hop IP
Default  10.0.0.0/16      Virtual network      -
User     10.0.2.0/24      Virtual appliance    10.0.9.4
User     10.0.2.128/25    None                 -
Default  0.0.0.0/0        Internet             -
User     0.0.0.0/0        Virtual appliance    10.0.9.4

For each destination, select the next hop that is used.
items.instr: To answer, select the appropriate option in each row.
items.answerText: 10.0.1.10 → Virtual network; 10.0.2.20 → Virtual appliance 10.0.9.4; 10.0.2.200 → None (dropped); 8.8.8.8 → Virtual appliance 10.0.9.4
items.expl:
Correct selections:

  • 10.0.1.10 → Virtual network. Only 10.0.0.0/16 matches, so it uses the system Virtual network route.
  • 10.0.2.20 → Virtual appliance 10.0.9.4. 10.0.2.0/24 is the longest match.
  • 10.0.2.200 → None (dropped). 10.0.2.128/25 is longer than /24, and next hop None drops the packet.
  • 8.8.8.8 → Virtual appliance 10.0.9.4. Both 0.0.0.0/0 routes match. For equal prefixes, a user route overrides the system route.

Azure picks the route with the longest prefix match. When prefixes tie, user-defined routes win over BGP routes, which win over system routes.

Inbound NAT rules forward traffic arriving on a specific frontend IP and port to a specific backend instance and port. Allow 3389 on VM2's NSG too. Bastion is usually the more secure option.

items.stem:
A log-processing workload needs its storage account to survive the failure of a single datacenter (zone) in the region. Geographic replication isn't required, and cost must be minimized.

Which redundancy option should you choose?
items.answerText: D — Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
items.expl:
Correct answer: D — Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)

ZRS synchronously copies data across three availability zones in one region. That's the cheapest option that survives a zone failure.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — Locally redundant storage (LRS): keeps three copies in a single datacenter, so a zone failure can make data unavailable.
  • B — Geo-redundant storage (GRS): adds a secondary region but still uses LRS in the primary.
  • C — Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS): meets the requirement but adds secondary-region cost that isn't needed.

items.stem:
A custom role definition contains "Actions": ["Microsoft.Compute/*"] and "NotActions": ["Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete"]. A user has this custom role and the built-in Virtual Machine Contributor role on the same resource group.

Can the user delete a VM in that resource group?
items.answerText: B — Yes, because NotActions only removes permissions from that role and isn't a deny; Virtual Machine Contributor grants delete
items.expl:
Correct answer: B — Yes, because NotActions only removes permissions from that role and isn't a deny; Virtual Machine Contributor grants delete

NotActions subtracts actions from the same role's Actions; it isn't a deny assignment. Effective permissions are the union across roles, so delete is allowed through Virtual Machine Contributor.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — Yes, but only if the custom role's AssignableScopes includes the subscription: AssignableScopes controls where a role can be assigned, not how NotActions combines with other roles.
  • C — No, because NotActions in any assigned role denies the action: this is the misconception being tested; only deny assignments block an action granted elsewhere.
  • D — No, because custom roles take precedence over built-in roles: there's no precedence between roles; RBAC is additive.

References

  • azure/role-based-access-control/custom-roles
  • azure/role-based-access-control/deny-assignments

items.stem:
A data disk for a transactional database needs sub-millisecond latency and IOPS and throughput that you can change on the fly without resizing the disk.

Which disk type should you use?
items.answerText: A — Ultra Disk
items.expl:
Correct answer: A — Ultra Disk

Ultra Disks deliver sub-millisecond latency and let you adjust IOPS and throughput independently of capacity without detaching the disk. They're supported as data disks only.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B — Standard SSD: designed for lighter workloads with lower, size-based performance.
  • C — Standard HDD: for backup and noncritical workloads with the highest latency.
  • D — Premium SSD: performance is tied to the disk size tier (with optional bursting), not independently adjustable.

Note: Premium SSD v2 also offers adjustable performance and is a valid answer in many real designs; it wasn't offered as an option here.

A team must be prevented from deploying VM sizes outside the D-series in resource group RG-Batch. Other resource groups must not be affected.

What should you do?
items.answerText: B — Assign the built-in Allowed virtual machine size SKUs policy at RG-Batch with the permitted D-series sizes
items.expl:
Correct answer: B — Assign the built-in Allowed virtual machine size SKUs policy at RG-Batch with the permitted D-series sizes

Allowed virtual machine size SKUs is a built-in Deny policy. Assigning it at the resource group scope limits only RG-Batch.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — Apply a CanNotDelete lock to RG-Batch: locks don't constrain VM size.
  • C — Reduce the subscription vCPU quota for non-D families: quotas are per subscription and region, so they'd affect every resource group.
  • D — Create a custom RBAC role without Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write: this would block all VM creation, not just sizes outside the D-series.

You need daily, snapshot-based operational backups of several Azure managed disks, with incremental snapshots kept in your own resource group.

Which vault type should you create?
items.answerText: C — Backup vault
items.expl:
Correct answer: C — Backup vault

Azure Disk Backup is managed through a Backup vault, which handles newer workloads such as Azure Disks, Blobs and Azure Database for PostgreSQL. Recovery Services vaults handle Azure VMs, SQL/SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files and MARS.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — Storage account with soft delete: isn't a backup orchestration service.
  • B — Key vault: stores secrets and keys, not backups.
  • D — Recovery Services vault: doesn't host the Azure Disk Backup workload.

A Bicep file must create three resource groups and then deploy resources into each one in a single deployment.

How should you configure and deploy the file?
items.answerText: D — Set targetScope = 'subscription' and deploy with New-AzSubscriptionDeployment, using modules scoped to each resource group
items.expl:
Correct answer: D — Set targetScope = 'subscription' and deploy with New-AzSubscriptionDeployment, using modules scoped to each resource group

Resource groups are subscription-level resources. A file with targetScope = 'subscription' can create them and call modules with scope: resourceGroup(...) to deploy inside them. Subscription deployments use New-AzSubscriptionDeployment (alias New-AzDeployment).

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — Keep the default targetScope and deploy with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment: a resource group deployment can't create resource groups.
  • B — Create the resource groups with dependsOn in a resource group deployment: dependsOn doesn't change the deployment scope.
  • C — Set targetScope = 'tenant' and deploy with New-AzTenantDeployment: tenant scope is for management groups and tenant-level resources and needs extra permissions.

References

VMs in VNet-App must be resolvable by host name (for example, vm-app1.corp.contoso.internal), and the DNS records must be created and removed automatically as VMs come and go.

What should you configure?
items.answerText: C — A private DNS zone named corp.contoso.internal with a virtual network link to VNet-App that has auto-registration enabled
items.expl:
Correct answer: C — A private DNS zone named corp.contoso.internal with a virtual network link to VNet-App that has auto-registration enabled

Auto-registration on a private DNS zone's VNet link automatically creates A records for VMs in the linked VNet and removes them when the VMs are deleted.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — A private DNS zone linked to VNet-App without auto-registration: resolution works, but records must be created manually.
  • B — Custom DNS servers set on the VNet pointing to 168.63.129.16: this is Azure-provided DNS, which doesn't use a custom zone name.
  • D — A public DNS zone with A records for each VM: the records would be public and manual.

  • azure/dns/private-dns-overview

items.objective: Configure Azure Files and Azure Blob Storage
items.stem:
Financial records in container ledger must not be modified or deleted for seven years after they're written, and even account administrators must not be able to shorten that period once it's locked.

What should you configure?
items.answerText: D — A locked time-based retention immutability policy of seven years on the container
items.expl:
Correct answer: D — A locked time-based retention immutability policy of seven years on the container

A time-based retention policy puts blobs in a WORM (write once, read many) state for the specified interval. Once locked, the policy's retention period can't be shortened, which meets SEC-style compliance requirements.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — Blob soft delete with 365-day retention: soft delete allows modification and has a maximum retention of 365 days.
  • B — A legal hold on the container: legal holds have no time period and are cleared manually.
  • C — A CanNotDelete resource lock on the storage account: management-plane locks don't stop data-plane writes or deletes of blobs.

References

  • azure/storage/blobs/immutable-storage-overview

items.objective: Manage Microsoft Entra users and groups
items.stem:
Contoso has offices in Paris and Berlin. The Paris helpdesk must be able to reset passwords only for users who work in Paris. Least privilege is required.

What should you implement?
items.answerText: A — An administrative unit that contains the Paris users, with the Helpdesk Administrator role assigned to the Paris helpdesk scoped to that administrative unit
items.expl:
Correct answer: A — An administrative unit that contains the Paris users, with the Helpdesk Administrator role assigned to the Paris helpdesk scoped to that administrative unit

Administrative units restrict the scope of Entra role assignments to a subset of users, groups, or devices. Assigning Helpdesk Administrator at the AU scope lets the Paris team reset passwords for Paris users only.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B — A security group of Paris users with the Helpdesk Administrator role assigned to that group: assigning a role to a group gives its members the role; it doesn't limit which users they can manage.
  • C — A management group named Paris with the User Access Administrator role: management groups organize Azure subscriptions; they don't scope Entra directory roles.
  • D — The Helpdesk Administrator role assigned at the tenant scope with a Conditional Access policy for Paris: tenant scope covers every user; Conditional Access doesn't restrict which accounts an admin can manage.

References

  • entra/identity/role-based-access-control/administrative-units
  • entra/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference

Which command should you run?
items.answerText: C — Get-AzRoleAssignment -SignInName kai@contoso.com -ExpandPrincipalGroups
items.expl:
Correct answer: C — Get-AzRoleAssignment -SignInName kai@contoso.com -ExpandPrincipalGroups

-ExpandPrincipalGroups makes Get-AzRoleAssignment return assignments made directly to the user and to groups the user belongs to. Without it you see direct assignments only.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — Get-MgUserMemberOf -UserId kai@contoso.com: lists group memberships, not Azure RBAC assignments.
  • B — Get-AzRoleAssignment -SignInName kai@contoso.com: returns direct assignments only and misses group-based access.
  • D — Get-AzRoleDefinition -Name kai@contoso.com: returns role definitions, not assignments, and doesn't accept a user.

items.stem:
You over-provisioned a 1 TiB Premium SSD data disk on VM1 and want to reduce it to 256 GiB to save money.

What should you do?
items.answerText: C — Create a new 256 GiB disk, copy the data to it, and replace the original disk
items.expl:
Correct answer: C — Create a new 256 GiB disk, copy the data to it, and replace the original disk

Azure managed disks can't be shrunk. You can only increase size. To reduce cost, create a smaller disk, migrate the data inside the guest, and remove the larger disk.

Why the other options are wrong

  • A — Deallocate VM1 and set the disk size to 256 GiB: decreasing size isn't supported, even when deallocated.
  • B — Take an incremental snapshot and restore it as 256 GiB: a disk created from a snapshot can't be smaller than the source.
  • D — Change the disk performance tier to P15: the tier can be raised for performance but can't go below the tier that matches the provisioned size, and capacity stays 1 TiB.

References

  • azure/virtual-machines/windows/expand-disks
  • azure/virtual-machines/disks-types

items.stem:
You are creating a new resource group named RG-Payments.

Which two statements about resource groups are true?
items.instr: Choose 2. Each correct selection presents part of the solution.
items.answerText: A, D
items.expl:
Correct answers: A, D

Resource groups are logical containers. Their location only affects metadata, and each resource belongs to exactly one group.

  • A — A resource can belong to only one resource group at a time: resources are in exactly one group, and they can be moved.
  • D — A resource group stores metadata about its resources in the region you choose for the group: the resource group location is where its metadata is stored.

Why the other options are wrong

  • B — Resource groups can be nested inside other resource groups: resource groups can't be nested.
  • C — All resources in a resource group must be in the same region as the group: resources in a group can be in different regions.
  • E — Deleting a resource group leaves its resources in place: deleting a group deletes everything in it.

References

  • azure/azure-resource-manager/management/manage-resource-groups-portal
